title: The Isma'ilis
hook: a Shia community led today by a living Imam, the Aga Khan, known for development work

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shia communities today. Your line: shia around the world. Which country did you find on the map? Yesterday also named the Isma'ilis as one Shia branch. Today, a closer look. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-five.

What happens when a question comes up that nobody in the first centuries ever faced? A new medicine. A new kind of work. A family that has moved to a country with different laws. Muslim communities have their own ways of answering. Some open the books of the schools. Some ask a mufti. Some ask a marja'. One community answers in a way that surprises people meeting it for the first time: they turn to a living Imam, a descendant of the Prophet's family, whom they recognize as the guide for their own time. His title is the Aga Khan. The community is the Isma'ilis.
screen: `A QUESTION NOBODY FACED BEFORE.` → `BOOKS, MUFTI, MARJA'.` → `A LIVING IMAM.`

segments.voice: First, where they come from. Isma'ilis are Shia Muslims who trace their line of Imams through Isma'il, a son of the Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, and they take their name from him. Twelver Shia followed a different son, which is how the two branches part. Second, the living Imam. The Isma'ilis described here hold that the line of Imams has never been broken, and that there is always a present Imam, the Imam of the time. They point to a verse in surah al-Nisa, in Pickthall's words: "Obey Allah, and obey the messenger and those of you who are in authority". For them, those in authority include the Imam. Sunni scholars read the same words differently, as rulers or people of knowledge. Each reads it in its own tradition. Third, the life of the community. Isma'ilis gather in a jamatkhana, a house for the community's prayer and meeting. In South Asian communities, devotional songs called ginans are part of that life. Isma'ilis speak of the outward form of faith and its inward meaning, and see the Imam as a guide to both. Fourth, the work. The Imam has built institutions grouped as the Aga Khan Development Network: schools, hospitals, rural support, care for historic buildings, help in places of poverty, open to people of every faith. Isma'ilis explain this as faith that cares for life in this world as well as the next. Volunteering, giving time and skill, is woven through the community's life.
screen: `THROUGH ISMA'IL, SON OF JA'FAR.` · `THE IMAM OF THE TIME.` · `JAMATKHANA AND GINANS.` · `SCHOOLS, CLINICS, VILLAGES.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn about their work. Start with the idea underneath it, that care for people's daily lives can be a form of devotion. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place that served you without asking who you were: a school, a clinic, a library, a shelter. See the building. See one person who worked there. Stay with that picture for a few breaths, and let gratitude be simple. If you pray, you can thank Allah for that place in your own words. Later today, read about one project of the Aga Khan Development Network, a school or a clinic, and notice who it serves. The bell holds the time.
The Isma'ilis. Shia Muslims who follow a living Imam, today the Aga Khan, gather in the jamatkhana, and are known for development work open to everyone. Today's word.

Your line: a living imam. Today, notice one person whose guidance you follow without thinking about it, and ask what makes you trust them. Tomorrow, converts and reverts. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Isma'ili Muslims recognize a living Imam, the Aga Khan, as the guide of their time; they gather for prayer in a jamatkhana, and the community supports the Aga Khan Development Network's schools, hospitals and rural programs with volunteered time and giving.

what it means: the title of the living Imam of the Isma'ilis, a Shia community that looks to him as the guide of its time.

sources.quoted: Obey Allah, and obey the messenger and those of you who are in authority

notes: This describes the Nizari Isma'ilis, who follow the Aga Khan; other Isma'ili communities (for example the Musta'li Bohras) follow a different line and have no present Imam in the same sense. The teach says 'the Isma'ilis described here'; a Keeper may want a clearer line on this.
No count of Imams, no dates and no succession details are given, because the outline's text does not supply them; the Aga Khan is named only by title.
The list of AKDN fields (schools, hospitals, rural support, historic buildings) should be confirmed against AKDN's own description.
The reading of 4:59 as including the Imam, and the Sunni reading as rulers or people of knowledge, should be checked by scholars of each.
Editor: fixed an ambiguous 'they' (ginans vs Isma'ilis) on the outward and inward meaning of faith; the teach no longer refers to 'the outline' aloud.
